title: What Makes Content Quotable by AI? The Anatomy of a Passage Engines Lift
metaTitle: What Makes Content Quotable by AI: Passage Anatomy
metaDescription: A quotable passage names its subject, makes one specific claim and carries a dated, sourced number. Six traits, three before-and-after rewrites and a checklist.
shortAnswer: A passage is quotable when it still makes sense alone: it names its subject, makes one specific claim, backs it with a dated, sourced number, and sits under a heading that asks the question it answers. Engines retrieve and cite passages, not whole pages, so a sentence that leans on its neighbours gets skipped. Test each key passage by pasting it, with its heading, into a blank document.
intro:
Quotable is a property of a passage, not a page. When Anthropic's web search tool cites a source, it [returns up to 150 characters of cited text](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool), roughly one sentence. That sentence has to survive without the paragraph around it.

Most uncited pages are not badly written. They are written for a reader who has already read the previous paragraph. This page is the anatomy of one passage; for the page-level process, see our [guide to optimizing content for AI search](/guides/how-to-optimize-content-for-ai-search).

One caveat first: Google says you do not need to [write in a special way for AI](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide). Everything below is plain good writing that also survives extraction.

sections.heading: What makes a passage quotable by AI?
sections.body:
A quotable passage is self-contained, specific, sourced, structured, dated and entity-explicit. Each trait removes one reason for an engine to skip you: missing context, a vague claim, an unverifiable number, a buried answer, a stale fact or an ambiguous subject.

| Trait | Passes when | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Self-contained | It makes sense pasted alone | "As mentioned above", "this approach" |
| Specific | It holds a number, name or condition | "Fast", "many", "leading" |
| Sourced | A primary source is linked | "Studies show" |
| Structured | The first sentence answers the heading | The answer arrives in paragraph four |
| Dated | It says when the fact was true | No date, or a stale one |
| Entity-explicit | It names the brand, product and period | "The company", "it", "last quarter" |

Microsoft asks for the same shape. Its guidance for Copilot-style assistants lists [self-contained phrasing, one-to-two-sentence answers and strong headings](https://about.ads.microsoft.com/en/blog/post/october-2025/optimizing-your-content-for-inclusion-in-ai-search-answers), and says assistants break pages into smaller pieces.

Anthropic shows why the last trait matters. In its [contextual retrieval write-up](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval), a chunk reading "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter" does not say which company or period, so it is hard to retrieve or use. A great page can still contain a worthless sentence.

![Side view of an open hardcover book with a worn spine and lit pages resting on a red surface.](https://images.pexels.com/photos/1988270/pexels-photo-1988270.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: Why does specificity matter most?
sections.body:
Specificity matters most because every other trait only delivers what the passage contains. Structure cannot rescue a vague claim, and a source cannot rescue a claim that says nothing. A vague claim is the commodity version of a sentence: Google defines [commodity content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) as common knowledge that could come from anyone.

Microsoft's advice is blunt: [avoid vague language and anchor claims in measurable facts](https://about.ads.microsoft.com/en/blog/post/october-2025/optimizing-your-content-for-inclusion-in-ai-search-answers). In the [GEO study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735), adding statistics, quotations and cited sources raised visibility in a research setting, while keyword stuffing did not. The numbers are in our [ranking factors page](/answers/ai-search-ranking-factors).

**Rewrite 1: from adjectives to evidence.** Illustrative example; Acme Helpdesk is a fictional brand and the figures are invented to show the pattern. Use only numbers you measured.

> **Before:** "Our support team is fast, friendly and loved by customers."
>
> **After:** "Acme Helpdesk answers 90% of tickets within two hours on weekdays, measured over the 12 months to September 2026."

The "before" could describe ten thousand sites. The "after" names the brand, a number, a period and a method, and only its owner can say it. That is why original data is the most quotable thing you can publish: nobody else has it. No data? Publish what only you know, such as prices, limits and steps you have tested.

sections.heading: How does structure affect whether a passage is found?
sections.body:
Structure decides whether an engine can find the claim and lift it whole. Put the answer in the first one or two sentences under a heading that asks the question, keep paragraphs short, and use lists or tables for parallel facts. Do not hide answers in tabs or expandable menus: Microsoft warns assistants [may not render hidden content](https://about.ads.microsoft.com/en/blog/post/october-2025/optimizing-your-content-for-inclusion-in-ai-search-answers).

There is mechanism behind answer-first. A 2025 [position-bias study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13950) found dense embedding and ColBERT-style retrievers lost 15.6% of performance on average when the relevant information appeared later in a passage; BM25 and reranker models were more robust. It tests research retrievers, not ChatGPT or Perplexity, so treat it as a reason, not proof.

**Rewrite 2: from pronouns to names.** Illustrative again, same fictional brand.

> **Before:** "It is included on the higher plan, as noted above, so this is the better pick for larger teams."
>
> **After:** "Acme Helpdesk includes single sign-on (SAML) only on its Business plan, so teams that require SSO must buy Business."

Pronouns such as "it" and "this" only resolve with context, a problem linguists call [coreference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coreference). Strip the context and the pronoun points at nothing.

Our position on chunking: write every section so it stands alone, because readers benefit too. But Google says there is [no requirement to break content into tiny pieces](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), so never fragment a page for engines.

sections.heading: How do sources and dates build trust?
sections.body:
Sources and dates let a reader, and a retrieval system, check a claim before repeating it. Attribute each number inline to a primary source with its year, and show a visible date that changes only when the facts do. A number with no source or date cannot be checked.

- **Source inline.** Write "according to X, month year" next to the number and link the original study, not a blog that summarized it.
- **Date visibly.** Google advises a [user-visible date labeled "Published" or "Last updated"](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/publication-dates), plus `datePublished` and `dateModified` in Article markup. It estimates the byline date from several signals, including significant updates.
- **Match your markup.** Google says structured data should [match the visible text](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). Schema cannot make a vague passage quotable; see our [structured data guide](/blog/structured-data-for-ai).

We refuse to bump a date on unchanged text. It misleads readers, and engines gain nothing from it.

**Rewrite 3: from a gesture to a dated, sourced fact.** This one uses a real claim.

> **Before:** "Google has some requirements for showing up in AI answers."
>
> **After:** "As of October 2026, [Google says](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) a page must be indexed and eligible to appear in Google Search with a snippet to be a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode."

Seven more rewrites, with the evidence behind each, are in [GEO examples](/blog/geo-examples).

![A woman and a man in blazers leaf through a stack of papers together outdoors.](https://images.pexels.com/photos/4964795/pexels-photo-4964795.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How do you test your own content for quotability?
sections.body:
Run a ten-minute test on your ten most important pages. Copy the first passage under each heading into a blank document and ask the seven questions below. A passage that fails any one gets rewritten before you publish another page.

1. **Paste test:** with only the heading and passage, would a stranger know who and what this is about?
2. **Name test:** is the brand or product named, with no stray "it", "they" or "the company"?
3. **Number test:** does each claim hold a number, name or condition?
4. **Source test:** is there a link to the primary source, with its year?
5. **Date test:** does the passage say when it was true?
6. **Answer test:** does the first sentence answer the heading?
7. **Fetch test:** can a bot reach the text? Check robots.txt, firewall rules and whether the answer sits in plain HTML.

The fetch test is not a formality. In [AEOeye's crawler access study](/blog/ai-crawler-user-agent-directory) (October 2026; 391 well-known sites, a convenience sample), 24 of 88 e-commerce and consumer homepages challenged our self-identified crawler. Quotable text behind a bot wall is not quotable.

Then ask the engines. [AEOeye's free audit](/) puts three unbranded buyer questions to ChatGPT live, shows the real answers and lists the competitors named instead of you.

Finally, one page per question. On 2026-10-03 we merged 165 AEOeye pages into 42, and we stand by the lesson: one strong page per question beats five thin ones.

keyTakeaways: Quotable is a property of a passage: it must still make sense, with its heading, when read alone.
Six traits: self-contained, specific, sourced, structured, dated and entity-explicit. Specificity is the one structure cannot fake.
Name the brand, product and period; pronouns and phrases like "as mentioned above" break once a passage is lifted out.
Source numbers inline, show a real date, and change it only when the facts change.
Test with a blank document, then confirm bots can fetch the text at all.

faqs.q: How long should a quotable passage be?
faqs.a: Make the core claim one or two sentences. Microsoft asks for one-to-two-sentence answers, and Anthropic's web search tool returns up to 150 characters of cited text per citation. Supporting detail can follow. Our 40 to 60 word opening is a rule of thumb for headings, not a limit any engine publishes.

faqs.q: Do I need to rewrite my pages specially for AI?
faqs.a: Not in a special style. Google says you do not need to write a specific way for its AI features, and unique content matters most. What helps is ordinary clarity: name the subject, make claims specific, and cite sources. Those habits also help readers who land mid-page from a search result.

faqs.q: Do statistics make content more quotable?
faqs.a: Real, sourced, dated statistics do. In the GEO study, adding statistics, quotations or cited sources raised visibility in a research setting. An invented or undated number does harm, because neither readers nor engines can verify it. If you have no data, quote a named expert or publish your own measurements.

faqs.q: Does schema markup make a passage quotable?
faqs.a: No. Google says no special schema is needed for its AI features and that structured data should match the visible text. Markup can describe a good passage but cannot add specifics a vague one lacks. Write the text first, then add markup that mirrors it.

faqs.q: Should I break pages into small chunks for AI?
faqs.a: No. Google says there is no requirement to break content into tiny pieces. Microsoft describes headings as marking where one idea ends and another begins. Do that: one concept per heading, each section readable alone. Splitting one topic across many thin pages is worse, because it divides your best passage.

definitions.definition: When two or more expressions in a text refer to the same person or thing, such as a brand name and the later word "it"; resolving it often needs context a lifted passage no longer has.

Google's term for content built on common knowledge that could come from anyone and adds little unique insight, as opposed to non-commodity content with first-hand experience or a distinct point of view.
A technique where a language model retrieves relevant passages from documents or the web at answer time and uses them to write its response.
